tldr: We developed RAIWAY, a bipedal robot with large 20-inch wheels, and showed that distilling detailed in-simulation wheel contact information into a latent representation enables continuous rolling locomotion over rocky terrain and outdoor stairs up to 15 cm high without any exteroceptive or direct contact sensing.
hero_caption: Real-world experiments of RAIWAY traversing diverse and challenging environments: rushing down steep stairs (A), steep slopes (B, C), a gravel bed (D), a studded ramp (E), rocky terrain (F, G), and continuous ascent of outdoor staircases with 9 cm, 14 cm, and 15 cm riser heights (H, I, J). All traversed using the exact same policy and purely blind, continuous rolling locomotion.
overview:
Wheeled-legged robots combine wheels and legs. They attract attention as hybrid platforms that offer both high-speed, high-efficiency rolling on flat ground and legged traversability over rough terrain. However, most existing platforms stop wheel rotation when encountering obstacles, switching to stepping behaviors where legs lift up to use wheels as footholds. This sacrifices the natural speed and energy efficiency of rolling.

The research team asked: instead of stepping over obstacles, why not simply roll over them using the driving power of large wheels and tire compliance? To realize this, they built RAIWAY, a bipedal robot equipped with 20-inch (approx. 51 cm) off-road bicycle tires. However, rolling across irregular obstacles is strongly contact-dominated, governed by local contact mechanics between the tire surface and terrain. Covering the entire surface of a continuously rotating wheel with sensors is impractical, and vision sensors cannot see the contact patch itself.

To tackle this challenge, this paper proposes a learning framework that compresses rich multi-contact events available in simulation into a latent representation, and trains the controller to infer this representation online from proprioceptive history (joint encoders and IMU) during deployment. In real-world validation, despite being completely blind without exteroceptive or tactile sensing, RAIWAY smoothly rolled through outdoor staircases up to 15 cm high, rocky fields, steep slopes, and gravel beds, significantly outperforming baselines that lack contact latent representations.
contributions: Developed RAIWAY, an in-house 6-DoF wheeled bipedal robot equipped with 20-inch large off-road tires and closed-cell polymer foam inserts, physically capable of rolling over obstacles.

Proposed a processing pipeline that transforms noisy and discontinuous multi-contact events in simulation into a fixed-length structured vector via rotation-invariant coordinate transformation, temporal filtering, and angular sorting, distilling them into a latent representation.

Demonstrated in real-world experiments that online inference of the contact state purely from proprioceptive history enables continuous traversal across steep slopes, gravel beds, rocky terrain, and staircases up to 15 cm high using a single blind policy.

sections.heading: Why stop stepping and start rolling over obstacles with large wheels?
sections.summary: Many wheeled-legged robots rely on stepping motions using wheels as footholds over obstacles, losing the speed and efficiency of rolling. This study adopts 20-inch large wheels to roll directly over steps, resolving hard-to-measure wheel contact states through latent representation learning from simulation.
sections.details:
Legged robots can traverse rough terrain freely using articulated legs. On flat ground, however, wheeled robots are drastically faster and more energy-efficient. Wheeled-legged robots merging both are promising platforms. Yet when encountering obstacles or discontinuous terrain, most existing works adopt a strategy of treating wheels merely as footholds and lifting legs to step up stairs. This ruins the biggest advantage of wheels: continuous, high-speed, and energy-efficient rolling.

Things change if wheels are sufficiently large. A large radius provides a shallow approach angle against obstacle edges, and tire compliance absorbs impact forces. This physically enables the robot to surmount moderate obstacles purely through wheel drive. Therefore, the team developed RAIWAY, an in-house bipedal robot equipped with large 20-inch wheels.

The fundamental difficulty lies in the fact that rolling locomotion is contact-dominated. Overcoming an obstacle is extremely sensitive to local wheel-terrain interaction. However, instrumenting the entire circumference of a rapidly spinning wheel with contact sensors is practically unfeasible. Furthermore, exteroceptive sensors like cameras only look down at terrain geometry; they cannot see the actual contact patch where the tire engages the ground.

Prior works attempted to tune simulation contact models as close to reality as possible, but perfectly modeling the complex contact dynamics of deforming elastic tires is difficult. This study takes an alternative route: leveraging rich multi-contact information available only in simulation as a teacher, distilling contact states into a compact latent representation. At deployment, this latent representation is inferred online from the time-series history of proprioception (joint angles and IMU). Making full use of rich contact patterns enabled by large wheels as privileged information is the key highlight of this approach.

sections.heading: The evolution of wheeled bipeds and where privileged information matters in RL
sections.summary: Prior wheeled-legged robots solved obstacles via specialized leg motions such as jumping or contact-triggered leg lifting. While privileged information in reinforcement learning has succeeded in walking and manipulation, this work uniquely latents contact information specifically for contact-dominated rolling locomotion.
sections.details:
### II-A Existing Wheeled Bipeds and Blind Locomotion
Wheeled bipedal robots have been actively studied in recent years as platforms combining compact footprints with high mobility. Notable examples include Ascento, which leaps over obstacles using four-bar linkage legs; Ascento Pro, featuring serial 2-DoF legs that scale steps via RL or non-smooth trajectory optimization; and TRON1, which combines small wheels with high-DoF legs to trigger leg-lifting upon obstacle contact.
However, a common theme across these prior works is the explicit separation between wheeled rolling and leg clearance motions: rolling on flat ground, but switching to specialized leg maneuvers (jumping or stepping) for obstacles. In contrast, RAIWAY uses large off-road tires to directly roll over moderate obstacles via tire physics—shallow attack angles, impact absorption, and traction. The legs are designed not for stepping, but solely to maintain body posture and regulate load distribution.

### II-B Explicit Estimation vs. Implicit Adaptation of Privileged Information
In reinforcement learning (RL), training with privileged information available only in simulation to bridge the Sim-to-Real gap is a standard practice. This broadly splits into two paradigms: explicit estimation, where privileged quantities are directly predicted on the real robot, and implicit adaptation (such as ROA or RMA), where a compressed latent variable of privileged information is reconstructed from proprioceptive history.
Prior works on legged robots have used foot contact forces or normals as privileged signals, but these were merely one of many privileged variables (such as friction coefficients or base velocity). In large-wheel rolling locomotion, however, the problem itself is contact-dominated. Unlike point-contact feet, the spatially distributed contact patterns across a large wheel surface provide an exceptionally informative signal. Thus, this study builds an adaptation framework tailored specifically to this rich contact information.

sections.heading: Designing the RAIWAY robot and taming wild contact signals for learning
sections.summary: RAIWAY is a 6-DoF robot with 20-inch wheels and foam tire inserts. Severe chattering in simulated contact events is conditioned via rotation-invariant frames, temporal filtering, and angular sorting. An ROA-based teacher-student setup allows online latent contact inference from proprioception on hardware.
sections.details:
### III-A 20-inch Large-Wheeled Bipedal Robot: RAIWAY
RAIWAY is a bipedal robot with 6 degrees of freedom in total: 2 pitch joints and 1 wheel joint per leg (Fig. F2). It has no roll or yaw hip joints, steering entirely via differential wheel speeds. Major components—actuators, linkages, motor drivers, and power electronics—are reused from the proven quadruped robot RAIBO2, with a newly designed chassis frame for the bipedal configuration. Total mass including battery is roughly 28 kg, standing at 1.14 m. It carries an onboard Jetson AGX Orin computer and a MicroStrain IMU.
The centerpiece is the drive wheels. 20-inch off-road bicycle tires are directly coupled to actuator output shafts. Instead of inner tubes, they are filled with closed-cell polymer foam inserts. Pneumatic tires suffer from unpredictable impact behaviors—bouncing when over-inflated or pinch-flatting the rim when under-inflated. Foam inserts maintain consistent deformation and rebound during collisions. This predictability greatly suppresses Sim-to-Real gaps in contact dynamics.

### III-B Contact-Informed Control Framework
The control policy integrates three components: recurrent encoding of proprioception, explicit estimation of physical quantities, and adaptation via contact latent representations (Fig. F3). Commands given to the robot are target forward velocity and turning rate. Observations include base angular velocity, gravity vector, leg joint positions/velocities, and past two-step actions.
A GRU processes these inputs into features, while an explicit MLP estimator predicts physical variables $\mathbf{e}_t$ including base linear velocity, height, wheel clearances, lateral velocities, and slip metrics measuring deviation from ideal rolling. The contact latent representation $\tilde{\mathbf{l}}_t$, the core of this method, is then concatenated before the final actor MLP outputs target positions for the 4 leg joints and target velocities for the 2 wheels.

### III-C In-Simulation Contact Event Conditioning
Raw contact data (positions and impulses) from the simulator (Raisim) cannot be used directly due to severe chattering and discontinuities inherent to rigid-body contact simulations. We condition them in three stages:

1. **Rotation-Invariant Transformation**: We define a stationary wheel frame $\{W_s\}$ independent of wheel spin angle. Setting the axle as the $y$-axis and opposite gravity as the $z$-axis fixed on the wheel plane ensures contact positions are geometrically uniquely defined regardless of how fast the wheel rotates.
2. **Temporal Filtering**: When contact occurs, it registers immediately in 1 sub-step. When contact is lost, an asymmetric debounce filter requires 25 consecutive sub-steps (62.5 ms) without contact before considering it detached. This aggressively filters out simulation chattering during steady rolling (Fig. F4).
3. **Angular Sorting and Fixed-Length Padding**: Filtered contacts are sorted by angle around the wheel circumference into 3 fixed slots. If more than 3 contacts occur, the closest points are merged. Geometrical roles naturally align with slot order—lowest contact for flat rolling, forward contact for obstacle edge engagement—making the vector straightforward for neural networks to process.

This conditioned contact vector $\mathbf{c}_t$ is fed into a teacher LSTM operating at 400 Hz (4x the 100 Hz policy frequency) to produce contact latent $\mathbf{l}_t$. A student MLP learns to predict this latent $\tilde{\mathbf{l}}_t$ from a 20-step history of observations and actions using the ROA algorithm.

### III-D Training Details and Reward Design
Training uses PPO in Raisim across 200 parallel environments for 60,000 iterations (approx. 42 hours). Domain randomization covers wheel collision parameters, terrain friction, and restitution. In reward design, typical legged rewards like foot clearance and gait guidance were intentionally removed. Instead, wheel airtime penalties (rewarding ground contact) and slip-minimization rewards guide the policy to roll continuously with wheels rather than step with legs.

captions.F3: Overview of the proposed contact-informed policy learning framework. Raw contact events from simulation are structured into vector $c_t$ via coordinate transformation, temporal filtering, and angular sorting, then encoded into latent $l_t$ by a teacher LSTM. A student MLP infers this latent $\tilde{l}_t$ from proprioceptive history during real-world deployment.
captions.F4: Effect of temporal filtering during simulated locomotion across flat ground, stairs, and obstacles. Raw signals (blue) flicker heavily even on flat ground, while filtered signals (red) via the asymmetric debounce filter suppress chattering while smoothly capturing contact transitions at stair edges.

sections.heading: Rolling through 16 cm single steps, rough rock fields, and 15 cm stairs
sections.summary: In ablation studies, the proposed method achieved a 100% success rate on 16 cm steps and boosted rocky field traversal from 39% to 88%. Real-world outdoor trials demonstrated continuous blind traversal over slopes, gravel, studded surfaces, and staircases up to 15 cm high with a single policy.
sections.details:
### IV-A In-Simulation Analysis of Contact Vector and Latent Representation
We first conducted ablation tests on elements of contact vector $\mathbf{c}_t$ in simulation on a 15 cm stair-climbing task (1,000 trials). Removing contact position or impulse dropped traversal rates from 74.4% down to 50–53%, and reducing slot counts to 1 or 2 caused significant performance degradation. Retaining position and impulse across all 3 slots is critical for high performance.
Furthermore, Integrated Gradients attribution analysis revealed that contact positions accounted for 50.5% of the influence on the latent representation, with impulses accounting for 13.8%, confirming that geometric contact locations play a dominant role in control.

### IV-B Real-World Ablation: 16 cm Step and Rocky Terrain
Real-world evaluations evaluated climbing a single 16 cm step (~63% of wheel radius, 20 trials) and traversing a 20 m rocky course back and forth with erratic contacts (5 trials). Baselines included Plain AC, AC + estimator (traditional explicit estimator only), Ours w/o Estimator, Ours w/o Filtering, and Ours.
The results were dramatic. While AC + estimator improved step climbing, its rocky terrain success rate was only 39%. In rocky terrain with chaotic contacts, scalar physical estimates drifted heavily, throwing off the policy. In contrast, Ours w/o Estimator (using contact latents) jumped to an 83% success rate on rocks. Combining both explicit estimation and contact latents, Ours reached 100% on the 16 cm step and a peak 88% on rocky terrain.
Examining internal data during a 16 cm step climb (Fig. F6), the latent distance metric $d_t$ spikes the moment the wheel hits the obstacle edge (T2). After a brief loss of ground contact during rebound (T3), $d_t$ gradually returns to baseline as the wheel rolls over the top.

### IV-C Outdoor Field Demonstrations
RAIWAY tackled diverse outdoor environments using the exact same policy without parameter retuning or mode switching (Fig. F1):

- **High-speed and continuous dynamic terrain**: Rushing down steep stairs (up to 1.0 m/s), ascending/descending grassy slopes, and rolling through gravel where tires sink. The robot maintained stable rolling without falling despite harsh impacts and sudden traction changes.
- **Irregular and studded terrain**: On studded concrete ramps and riverbed rocks, contact points are unpredictable. As shown in Fig. F7, when the left wheel climbed a rock and spun freely, the slip estimator and contact latents responded instantly, stabilizing posture to clear the rock.
- **Periodic obstacles (stairs)**: The robot smoothly ascended stairs with 9 cm risers at 0.51 m/s average (0.62 m/s peak). On challenging 14 cm outdoor stairs, it achieved 11 consecutive round-trip ascents and descents. On 15 cm stairs, it topped 3 out of 10 runs (85.4% per-step success rate).

### IV-D Failure Mode Analysis
Experiments revealed two main failure modes. The first is surface texture and edge discrepancies. Indoor 16 cm wooden steps had sharp edges that gripped tire tread blocks well, yielding 100% success. Conversely, outdoor 15 cm granite stairs had rounded, polished edges, causing tires to slip and pitch the robot forward. Rigid-body simulators cannot capture micro-scale tread interlocking.
The second failure mode is high-frequency oscillation from wheel rebound. The real tire has a relatively high restitution coefficient (~0.61). However, training with high restitution makes policies overly hesitant, so restitution was capped at 0.3 in simulation. Consequently, severe impacts on hardware exposed the robot to out-of-distribution observation sequences, inducing leg torque oscillations that occasionally caused falls.

captions.F6: Time-series response during real-world 16 cm step ascent. Right after collision at T2, wheel speed drops and latent distance metric $d_t$ spikes. Following airtime from rebound at T3, the latent clearly captures contact transitions through completion (T5).
captions.F7: Real-world robot responses to sharp outdoor contact events: (a) Left wheel mounting a large rock and slipping before clearing (i–iv), and (b) Lateral wheel slip on a studded slope. The slip/lateral velocity estimators and latent variables ($l_3, l_4$) respond rapidly to recover posture.

sections.heading: Summary and look ahead: rolling through obstacles without looking down
sections.summary: Combining large wheels with contact latent representations enabled RAIWAY to achieve continuous rolling locomotion across challenging terrain without vision or contact sensors. Future work aims to integrate exteroceptive sensors like cameras to fuse advance terrain awareness with contact adaptation.
sections.details:
This work presented RAIWAY, an in-house bipedal robot with large 20-inch wheels, and a blind control framework leveraging multi-contact simulation data. To tackle the unique challenges of rolling locomotion—where covering wheels with sensors is impractical and exact contact dynamics are hard to model—we structured contact events into a latent representation inferred online from proprioceptive history.

Real-world experiments demonstrated that the robot can traverse steep slopes, gravel, rocky fields, and outdoor stairs up to 15 cm (over half the wheel radius) purely by continuous rolling, without stepping. Overcoming obstacles through wheel drive rather than stepping proved exceptionally effective on a large-wheeled platform.

Looking ahead, integrating exteroception (cameras, LiDAR) is a key direction. Combining predictive terrain awareness—anticipating obstacle shapes ahead—with contact-adaptive control that absorbs unexpected shocks underfoot will enable robots to conquer larger discontinuous terrain at even higher speeds.

takeaways: In wheeled bipedal robots, using sufficiently large wheels (20-inch in this work) allows the robot to roll directly through obstacles without stepping.

Rather than attempting to model complex tire compliance perfectly, distilling in-simulation multi-contact data into latent representations and inferring them online from proprioception is highly effective for Sim-to-Real transfer.
To handle rigid-body contact chattering, asymmetric temporal filtering (instant detection, gradual decay) and angular sorting are crucial to stabilize training.

While explicit scalar estimators work well for isolated single steps, they degrade under chaotic contacts like rocky fields. Complementing them with implicit contact latents maximizes hardware robustness.
limitations: On rounded stone edges or polished rocks where tire blocks cannot mechanically grip, discrepancies with rigid-body simulation persist, risking slip-induced falls.
Real tire restitution (~0.61) was higher than the training cap (0.3), meaning heavy impacts can expose the policy to out-of-distribution observations and induce high-frequency torque oscillations.
Because control is purely blind, the robot cannot decelerate or avoid obstacles that exceed its physical rolling clearance, highlighting the necessity of future vision integration.
